- (r1,c1,ch0) 2.697  
- (r2,c1,ch0) -3.588  
- (r6,c1,ch0) 2.234  
- (r7,c1,ch0) 1.790  
- (r8,c1,ch0) 2.358  

This means the agent is confined to the leftmost playable column, i.e. a vertical paddle on the left edge.  
Channel 1 (moving objects) has large weights spread across the grid, e.g.  
- (r5,c4,ch1) 4.754  
- (r6,c3,ch1) 3.495  
- (r7,c2,ch1) -3.103  
- (r8,c5,ch1) -3.351  
- (r2,c8,ch1) 1.616  

This suggests a ball moving through the playfield and possibly an opponent paddle on the right side.  
Channel 4 (previous frame) is heavily used, e.g.  
- (r1,c5,ch4) 5.236  
- (r8,c5,ch4) -4.515  
- (r3,c3,ch4) 3.882  

This indicates the network needs velocity/direction information from the previous frame.  
There are no meaningful top-8 connections from channel 2 (reward targets) or channel 3 (obstacles), so there are no internal reward cells or obstacles beyond the wall border.

Reasoning: The agent being fixed to column 1 rules out games where the agent roams the grid or moves horizontally along the bottom, such as Breakout, Space Invaders, Freeway, Pac-Man, Snake, or Frogger. A vertical paddle on the left, a moving ball, an opponent paddle on the right, only wall obstacles, and heavy use of the previous frame for velocity all match Pong. The absence of reward-target and obstacle channels is consistent with Pong, where reward is score-based rather than a cell.
